passages.title: The clear Book and the sign they never look at
passages.tafsir:
Surah Ash-Shu'ara opens by turning the camera around. We expect a rebuke of the deniers; instead the first words after the letters are addressed to the Prophet ﷺ himself, and they are words of consolation. These nine ayat hold together as one movement: a Book that could not be clearer (ayat 1–2), a Messenger grieving himself to pieces because people still will not accept it (ayah 3), Allah's explanation that He *could* force them but deliberately will not (ayah 4), the long human record of turning away from every fresh reminder (ayat 5–6), and then a sign lying under everyone's feet that they never bother to look at (ayat 7–8) — sealed with two names of Allah held together in one breath: the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful (ayah 9).

## The letters, and the Book that makes things clear (ayat 1–2)

The surah opens with **Ṭā Sīn Mīm** — three disconnected letters. Ibn Kathir does not re-open the question here. He simply notes that at the beginning of his explanation of Surat Al-Baqarah he discussed the letters which appear at the beginning of some surahs, and he lets that stand as his answer.

Ayah 2 then says: *"These are the verses of the clear Book."* The Arabic is **al-Kitāb al-Mubīn**. Ibn Kathir explains *mubīn* as **clear and unambiguous** — a Book that **distinguishes between truth and falsehood, and between misguidance and guidance**. Notice the two jobs packed into one word: the Book is clear *in itself*, and it *makes clear* what was previously blurred. Truth and falsehood do not arrive in the world already labelled; people mix them. This Book separates them.

Hold that thought against ayah 3, because the whole tension of the passage lives in the gap between them. The Book is *mubīn*. It is not obscure, not hard to make out. And yet people still walk away from it. The problem was never the clarity of the message.

## "You may destroy yourself" — the weight of *bākhiʿ* (ayah 3)

*"Perhaps you will grieve yourself to death over their not believing."*

The key word is **بَاخِعٌ (bākhiʿ)**. Ma'arif ul Qur'an opens the root for us: **bakhʿ** means *to reach up to the bikhāʿ — an artery of the neck — while slaughtering*. That is the literal picture: not a cut, but a cut driven all the way down to the deepest vessel. Applied here, Ma'arif says the word is used in the sense of **putting oneself into trouble and toil** — working oneself past the point of damage.

Ibn Kathir reads it just as strongly: *bākhiʿ nafsak* means **"destroy yourself"** — and he specifies the cause precisely: **because of your keenness that they should be guided, and your grief for them**. He then reports that **Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Qatadah, 'Atiyyah, Ad-Dahhak, Al-Hasan and others** glossed the phrase as **"kill yourself."** A whole line of early authorities, reaching for the strongest word available.

Pause on what Ibn Kathir's explanation reveals about him ﷺ. His grief is traced to *keenness that they should be guided*. The people mocking him were the ones he was agonising over.

Ibn Kathir places this alongside two sister verses: *"So destroy not yourself in sorrow for them"* (35:8), and *"Perhaps you would destroy yourself over their footsteps, because they believe not in this narration"* (18:6). Reading them together, he draws the conclusion plainly: **here Allah is consoling His Messenger ﷺ** for the lack of faith of those among the disbelievers who do not believe in him.

**A subtle grammatical point.** Ma'arif ul Qur'an cites **'Allamah 'Askari**: although at such places the sentence *appears* to be informative — "perhaps you are destroying yourself" — **it in fact means to prohibit or prevent**. It reads as a statement and lands as a gentle command. What it conveys, Ma'arif says, is: *"O Messenger, do not be so despondent because of your people's disbelief and rejection of Islam that you cause yourself to collapse."*

That is worth sitting with. The correction is wrapped inside an observation so tender it barely feels like a correction at all.

**Two lessons Ma'arif ul Qur'an draws from this ayah:**

1. **Even if it is apparent that a disbeliever would not convert to Islam, it is still not right to stop preaching to him.** The ayah restrains the Prophet's ﷺ *grief*, not his call.
2. **The efforts one makes for a certain objective must be balanced and moderate.** If someone is adamant not to be guided to the right path, **one should not be over-grieved**. The outcome was never your assignment.

## The sign that would bend their necks (ayah 4)

*"If We so will, We can send down to them a sign from the sky, before which their necks will stay bent in submission."*

Ibn Kathir's paraphrase is direct: **"if We so willed, We could send down a sign that would force them to believe, but We will not do that, because We do not want anyone to believe except by choice."** He supports this with *"And had your Lord willed, those on earth would have believed, all of them together. So will you then compel mankind, until they become believers?"* (10:99), and *"And if your Lord had so willed, He could surely have made mankind one Ummah"* (11:118).

So the deniers' refusal is not a failure of divine power. Allah is telling His Prophet ﷺ: I could end this argument in a moment. I have chosen not to. Ibn Kathir sums up the settled arrangement: **Allah's will has acted, His decree has come to pass, and His proof has been conveyed to mankind by the mission of Messengers and the revelation of Books to them.** Proof, not compulsion, is the mechanism.

**Why "their necks"?** Ma'arif ul Qur'an quotes **'Allamah Zamakhshari**: the real intent is that *the disbelievers themselves* will stay in submission, but the act of submission is attributed to their **necks** so that the initial object of submission is pinpointed — because **yielding or bowing in humility initially appears on the neck**. Submission is a whole-body act, but the neck is where it first shows, and that is the place the ayah names.

**And why does Allah withhold such a sign?** Ma'arif (citing Qurtubi) gives the reasoning. Allah has **full authority and control to evince any sign of His Oneness and Omnipotence** that would bring the religious injunctions and the Divine Truth forward **in such a self-evident manner that no one would have the ability to reject it**. But **wisdom demands** that these injunctions and the understanding of Allah are *not* made self-evident — that they remain dependent on **deliberations and pondering**. Why? Because **this pondering and deliberation is actually the test of man, on which the reward and punishment is adjudged.** And then the decisive line: **acceptance of self-evident things is a natural and involuntary phenomenon, which lacks the quality of deliberate obedience.**

Think of what a compelled faith would be worth. If the sky split and every neck bent, no one would have *chosen* anything. The very gap that lets a person deny is the same gap that makes belief a deliberate obedience. What looks like Allah's silence is the room He has left for your test.

## Turning away from every fresh reminder (ayat 5–6)

*"Whatever new reminder comes to them from the Most Compassionate, they turn away from it."*

Ibn Kathir renders the ayah as: *"And never comes there unto them a Reminder as a recent revelation from the Most Gracious, but they turn away therefrom."* Each reminder arrives fresh; the turning away is old. He reads the ayah as a statement about the human record: **every time a Scripture comes from heaven to them, most of the people turn away from it.**

Note too from whom it comes: **from ar-Rahmān, the Most Gracious**. Of all the names that could have been used here, that is the one the ayah chooses. What they turn from arrives under the name of mercy.

Ibn Kathir gathers the pattern from across the Qur'an: *"And most of mankind will not believe even if you desire it eagerly"* (12:103); *"Alas for mankind! There never came a Messenger to them but they used to mock at him"* (36:30); *"Then We sent Our Messengers in succession. Every time there came to a nation their Messenger, they denied him"* (23:44). Placed beside ayah 3, these have a consoling function: the Prophet ﷺ is not failing where others succeeded. He stands in a long line of messengers who met exactly this.

Ayah 6 then turns to the mockers: *"They have certainly denied, so the news of what they mocked at will come to them."* Ibn Kathir explains: **they denied the truth that came to them, so they will come to know the news of the consequences of this denial after a while.** The mockery does not evaporate; it matures. He connects this to the closing warning of this very surah — *"And those who do wrong will come to know by what overturning they will be overturned"* (26:227) — so the surah opens and closes on the same note.

## The sign they never look at (ayat 7–8)

*"Have they failed to look at the earth — how many of every noble kind We have caused to grow in it?"*

They demanded a sign from the sky. Allah points at the ground.

Ibn Kathir frames this as Allah's word to **those who dared to oppose His Messenger ﷺ and disbelieve in His Book**: He is **the Subduer, the Almighty, the All-Powerful, Who created the earth and caused every good kind of crop, fruit and animal to grow therein.**

**زَوْجٍ كَرِيمٍ (zawj karīm).** Ma'arif ul Qur'an unpacks both words. **Zawj** literally means **a pair** — which is why a man and a woman, and a male and a female, are each called *zawj*. Many species of trees have male and female among them, so on that basis they too can be called *zawj*. And the word *zawj* is sometimes used simply for **a special kind**, on which reading all species of trees can be called *zawj*. **Karīm**, Ma'arif says, means **a nice and favourite thing**.

So the ayah asks a question that answers itself. Every kind, in every pair, in endless variety, springing out of one dead ground. If you want a sign, you are standing on countless ones.

Ibn Kathir also relates that **Sufyan Ath-Thawri narrated from a man, from Ash-Sha'bi**, that **people are a product of the earth — so whoever enters Paradise is good and noble, and whoever enters Hell is base and vile.** The earth grows crops of differing worth; so does humanity. You are also something grown.

Ayah 8 draws the conclusion: **"Surely in this is a sign"** — which Ibn Kathir explains as **evidence of the power of the Creator of all things: He spread out the earth and raised the canopy of the heavens.** And then the ache: **"yet most of them would not believe"** — despite that, the majority do not believe, rather they **deny Him, His Messengers and His Books, and they go against His commands, doing the things He had prohibited.**

Set ayah 8 beside ayah 4 and the passage's argument closes. They will not believe when a compelling sign is *withheld*, and by Ma'arif's reasoning it would carry no deliberate obedience if one were *forced*. Meanwhile the sign is already growing outside the window, and they do not look.

## Al-'Azīz, ar-Rahīm (ayah 9)

*"And your Lord is certainly the Almighty, Most Merciful."*

The passage ends on two names. Ibn Kathir explains **al-'Azīz** as **the One who has power over all things, to subdue and control them** — so the deniers should not mistake delay for weakness. And he explains **ar-Rahīm** in a way that bears directly on that delay: He is merciful **towards His creation, for He does not hasten to punish the one who sins, but He gives him time to repent — and if he does not, then He seizes him with a mighty punishment.**

That is the answer to the whole passage. Why are the mockers still walking around unpunished? Not because Allah cannot — He is *al-'Azīz*. Because He is *ar-Rahīm*, and Ibn Kathir tells us what that delay is: time given to repent. Every day a denier is given is mercy, not oversight.

Ibn Kathir preserves how early scholars weighted the two names. **Abu Al-'Aliyah, Qatadah, Ar-Rabi' bin Anas and Ibn Ishaq** said of *al-'Azīz*: **"He is Almighty in His punishment of those who went against His commands and worshipped others besides Him."** And **Sa'id bin Jubayr** said of *ar-Rahīm*: **"He is Most Merciful towards those who repent to Him and turn to Him."** Two names, two doors, and the person facing them decides which he walks through.

Note also the word **رَبِّكَ — "*your* Lord."** After nine ayat about people who reject, the passage turns back to the Prophet ﷺ with a possessive. The consolation that opened the passage also closes it.

## Living it

**Carry the burden, not the outcome.** Ayah 3 lets you feel the full weight of caring about someone's guidance — and then, in the gentlest possible grammar, tells you not to let it destroy you. Ma'arif's two lessons are the practical shape of this: keep preaching even to the one who seems immovable, and keep your effort **balanced and moderate**, refusing to be over-grieved by a refusal that was never in your hands.

**Stop waiting for the sky to split.** Ayah 4 says the compelling sign is deliberately withheld, and the reasoning Ma'arif reports from Qurtubi tells you why: acceptance of the self-evident is involuntary and lacks the quality of deliberate obedience. So the ordinary state of the believer — pondering, deliberating, choosing without certainty forced upon him — is not a deficiency in your faith. Ma'arif says plainly that this pondering *is* the test.

**Look down.** Ayah 7 asks whether they ever actually *looked* at the earth. Signs go unnoticed not because they are hidden but because they are familiar. A pomegranate, a wheat field, a tree on your street — **every good kind** — each one is the argument, free and endless and ignored.

**Read the delay correctly.** Ayah 9 warns against two mistakes. Do not read Allah's patience with your own sins as indifference — Ibn Kathir says He gives the sinner time to repent, and Sa'id bin Jubayr says He is Most Merciful towards those who repent to Him and turn to Him. And do not read it as weakness either — He is *al-'Azīz*, with power over all things. The time you have been given is the mercy. Use it.

passages.title: Moses commissioned to face Pharaoh
passages.tafsir:
These eight ayat are the commissioning of Musa (peace be upon him): Allah calls him at the mountain and sends him to Pharaoh — a ruler who, as Maarif ul Quran describes him, was "claimant of being god" — Musa lays out honestly every reason he is afraid, Allah answers that fear in a single word, and the two brothers are handed the exact message they are to deliver.

What holds the passage together is that movement — **command (10–11), honest fear (12–14), divine reassurance (15), and the message itself (16–17)**. Nothing in the sequence is wasted. The fears are real and are spoken aloud; the answer is one word; the mission, when it finally comes, fits into two sentences.

## The call on the mountain (ayah 10)

Ibn Kathir sets the scene by stacking the verbs of what Allah did for Musa: Allah "called him from the right side of the mountain, and conversed with him, and chose him, sent him, and commanded him to go to Fir'awn and his people." Called, conversed, chose, sent, commanded — five acts, and the mission is the last of them, resting on everything before it.

And notice how Ibn Kathir introduces Musa in the same breath: "His servant, son of 'Imran and Messenger Musa, peace be upon him, **who spoke with Him**." Before Musa is a man with an assignment, he is a man Allah called, conversed with, and chose. That is the ground he is standing on when the hard command arrives.

## Two names for one people (ayat 10–11)

Musa is not told "go to Egypt" or "go to the king." He is told, *"Go to the people who are wrongdoers"* — and only then are they identified: *"The people of Fir'awn."* Ibn Kathir's text runs the two phrases straight together: the wrongdoers are Fir'awn's people.

The Qur'an does not leave that wrongdoing vague. By ayah 17 we learn exactly what it consisted of. Ibn Kathir describes the Children of Israel under Fir'awn as held in "captivity, subjugation and torture," in "a position of humiliating torture." Maarif ul Quran, citing Qurtubi, fills in the scale: they were originally residents of Syria who wanted to go back to their own land, and Pharaoh would not let them; four hundred years had passed with them living in his bondage like slaves; at that point they numbered six hundred and thirty thousand. So "wrongdoers" is not a label of abuse. It describes a state that had lasted four centuries.

Then the ayah ends not with a verdict but with a question: *"Will they not fear Allah?"* — Ibn Kathir's rendering keeps the Arabic word: *"Will they not have Taqwa?"* Of everything that could be said about a people who had enslaved a nation for four hundred years, what Allah names is the thing they lack. And He puts it as a question — which is how the door of the mission is opened rather than closed.

## Musa's fears, spoken plainly (ayat 12–14)

Musa does not say "yes" and he does not say "no." He tells his Lord, item by item, what frightens him:

- **"I fear that they will deny me"** (ayah 12) — in Maarif ul Quran's wording, "I fear they will belie me."
- **"And my breast straitens, and my tongue expresses not well"** (ayah 13). Maarif ul Quran renders the same words, "my heart gets straitened and my tongue is not fluent."
- **"So send for Harun"** (ayah 13).
- **"And they have a charge of crime against me, and I fear they will kill me"** (ayah 14). Ibn Kathir names the charge exactly: "because he had killed that Egyptian, which was the reason that he left the land of Egypt."

So the man being sent to Pharaoh is a man with a killing hanging over him in that very city, whose tongue "expresses not well" — and he is being sent to make an argument.

Ibn Kathir reads this alongside the fuller version of the same conversation in Surah Ta Ha: *"O my Lord! Open for me my chest. And ease my task for me"* (20:25–26), running through to Allah's reply, *"You are granted your request, O Musa!"* (20:36). As Ibn Kathir puts it, "Musa asked Allah to remove these difficulties for him." The narrowed chest and the tied tongue are not complaints thrown into the air. They are handed to the One who can open and ease them — and He does.

### Asking for help is not making excuses

Maarif ul Quran draws the principle out of exactly these three ayat, and it is worth pausing on, because Musa's words could sound like a man wriggling out of an assignment. They are not. Maarif ul Quran states that these verses show Musa "requested Allah to provide him with some resources to help them in carrying out his mission," and from this: "so far as the objective is to obey Allah's command, praying for some helping resources cannot be regarded as seeking ruses and excuses to escape from the required act. The request of Sayyidna Musa was only to facilitate the implementation of Allah's command which is quite lawful."

The test is in the direction of the request. Musa never asks to be released; every item on his list is aimed at getting the thing done. He does not say "send someone else" — he says **"send for Harun."** He wants a second voice, not an exit.

## "Nay!" — the answer to fear (ayah 15)

The whole list is met with one word: **كَلَّا** — rendered "Nay!" and "Certainly not!" Ibn Kathir's gloss is as direct as the word itself: "Allah told him: do not be afraid of anything like that."

Then comes what Allah actually gives.

**First, a brother.** Ibn Kathir cites the parallel promise, *"We will strengthen your arm through your brother, and give you both power"* (28:35) — and glosses that "power" with a single word: **"meaning, proof."** The reinforcement Allah supplies against a throne is an argument and a partner. And from this point in our passage the address is to two men, not one: *"Go you both with Our signs"*, *"And go both of you to Fir'awn, and say..."*

**Second, safety.** The same ayah continues, "so they shall not be able to harm you, with Our signs, you two as well as those who follow you will be the victors" (28:35) — victory extended past the two of them to everyone who follows.

**Third, and above all, Allah's own presence:** *"Go you both with Our signs. Verily, We shall be with you, listening."* Ibn Kathir sets this beside *"I am with you both, hearing and seeing"* (20:46), and explains the meaning: **"I will be with you by My protection, care, support and help."**

That is what the "withness" promised here amounts to, in Ibn Kathir's own words — not a distant awareness, but protection, care, support and help, for two men walking into a court that could kill them.

Notice, too, what the answer consists of. To *"they will deny me"*: signs. To *"they will kill me"*: "Nay" — and Allah listening. The fear is not argued away; it is outweighed.

## The message they carry (ayat 16–17)

The commission ends by putting the words in their mouths. Two sentences — one about who they are, one about what they want.

**"And go both of you to Fir'awn, and say: 'We are the Messengers of the Lord of Al-'Alamin'"** (ayah 16). Ibn Kathir reads it together with *"Verily, we are both Messengers of your Lord"* (20:47) and gives the sense: **"both of us have been sent to you."** Two men, one errand, one Sender.

And see how they are told to introduce themselves: not by their own names, and not even as messengers *to Pharaoh*, but as sent by the Lord of Al-'Alamin — which Ibn Kathir renders "the Lord of the all that exists." The title is itself the argument. The man who claimed to be god is addressed by two envoys of the One who owns everything that exists, Pharaoh included.

**"So allow the Children of Israel to go with us"** (ayah 17). This is the demand — the first concrete thing the mission asks of the tyrant. Ibn Kathir spells out its force: "let them go, free them from your captivity, subjugation and torture, for they are the believing servants of Allah, devoted to Him, and with you they are in a position of humiliating torture." And Maarif ul Quran, following Qurtubi, notes that when Musa presented the message of Truth to Pharaoh "he also asked him to stop all the cruelties he had perpetrated over Bani Isra'il and to let them go to their homeland."

So the call to the mightiest ruler of the age is not only *believe*; it is *release them*. The call to Allah alone and the freeing of the oppressed arrive in the same breath.

## Living it

**Fear does not disqualify you.** Musa says "I fear" twice in three ayat, in direct address to Allah, and he is still the one sent. What he does with the fear is take it to his Lord rather than let it decide for him.

**Ask for what will let you obey, not for a way out.** This is Maarif ul Quran's principle, and it is a usable test for our own hesitations: is my request aimed at doing the thing, or at escaping it? "Send for Harun" is the model — ask for the partner, the skill, the ease.

**Take a companion.** The strengthening Allah names against a throne is a brother at Musa's side. Do not weigh up a hard obedience without first asking who could stand in it with you.

**The support promised is proof and Allah's presence.** Ibn Kathir's one-word gloss on the "power" of 28:35 — "meaning, proof" — reframes what help from Allah looks like: signs and a clear argument, together with His "protection, care, support and help" while you walk toward the task.

**Do not hide your weakness.** Musa named the killing of the Egyptian to his Lord before Pharaoh could ever throw it at him. (Looking just past our passage, at ayat 18–22, Maarif ul Quran observes that when Pharaoh did throw it at him in open court, Musa took that charge up first rather than dodging it: "being the messenger of Allah, he had nothing to hide, so while replying he accepted his weakness" — the opposite of camouflaging a fault.)

**Speak for those who cannot speak.** Four hundred years of bondage; six hundred and thirty thousand people who wanted only to go home. When Allah finally sends a messenger to Pharaoh, their release is written into the very first speech.

passages.title: The favour thrown back at Pharaoh
passages.tafsir:
Two men have walked into the court of a king who claimed to be a god, and delivered a message. Pharaoh does not answer the message. He answers the man — dredging up Musa's (peace be upon him) childhood in his palace and the killing he fled from. These five ayat are that exchange: two accusations from Pharaoh (18–19), and Musa's reply in three moves (20–22), which ends by turning Pharaoh's boasted favour into the very charge against him.

## The setting

Ibn Kathir opens by telling us who was sent and by whom. Allah called His servant and Messenger Musa, son of ʿImran, peace be upon him — the one who spoke with Him — from the right side of the mountain, conversed with him, chose him, sent him, and commanded him to go to Pharaoh and his people. Musa's fear of that errand was concrete: "they have a charge of crime against me, and I fear they will kill me." Ibn Kathir states the reason plainly — **because he had killed that Egyptian, which was the reason that he left the land of Egypt.** So the accusation Pharaoh throws at him in ayah 19 is no ambush. Musa had named it to his Lord before he ever set out.

Allah's reply was "Nay!" — Ibn Kathir glosses it: do not be afraid of anything like that. Then: "Go you both with Our signs. Verily, We shall be with you, listening," which Ibn Kathir explains as *I will be with you by My protection, care, support and help.* Two men against an empire, with that as the guarantee.

Their demand was: "So allow the Children of Israel to go with us." Ibn Kathir: *let them go, free them from your captivity, subjugation and torture, for they are the believing servants of Allah, devoted to Him, and with you they are in a position of humiliating torture.*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Qurtubi, gives the scale of what was being asked. The Children of Israel were originally residents of Syria; they wanted to return to their land, and Pharaoh would not let them. **Four hundred years had passed** in that bondage, and by then they numbered **six hundred and thirty thousand.** Hold that number — it is the hinge on which ayah 22 turns.

## Pharaoh's move: attack the man, not the message

Ibn Kathir describes Pharaoh's reaction with devastating economy: **he turned away and ignored him completely, regarding him with scorn and thinking little of him.** He did not engage the claim that there is a Lord of all that exists. He changed the subject to Musa's biography.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names this for what it is. Debate between people of differing views — *munāzarah*, formal dialectic — is as old as humanity, but it has been reduced to a game of winning and losing: keep pressing your point even when you know you are wrong, and reject your opponent's point even when you know it is right. Islam, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, took a middle course and set rules for it, so that it becomes a useful tool for preaching and reform rather than a contest of egos. And when a sharp opponent lacks the correct arguments, **he switches the conversation to the person of the addressee, to find faults with him — a tactic used to embarrass him and make him look small before the audience.** That is exactly Pharaoh's move, and it is worth naming, because it is still the commonest way truth gets deflected in a room.

His two points, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays them out:

**First (ayah 18): the debt of upbringing.** *Did we not raise you among us as a child, and you stayed with us for years of your life?* Ibn Kathir unpacks the tone: "we brought you up among us, in our home and on our bed, we nourished you and did favors for you for many years, and after all that you responded to our kindness in this manner: you killed one of our men and denied our favors to you." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the unspoken sting into words: we have done so many favours to you, *so how can you have the face to speak before us?*

**Second (ayah 19): the killing.** *Then you did what you did.* Pharaoh's charge, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān phrases it, is that Musa killed an Egyptian for no fault of his: "this is not only cruelty but also ingratitude toward those among whom you are raised to your manhood. You have killed one from among us."

Then the label the ayah ends on: *wa anta min al-kāfirīn*, rendered here "being utterly ungrateful". Ibn Kathir gives the sense: **"one of those who deny favors"** — a reading he attributes to Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿAbdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam, noting it was the view favoured by Ibn Jarir. Pharaoh, who was himself a claimant to godhood, is charging Musa with ingratitude. The irony is not lost, and Musa will use it.

## Musa's reply — and the order he chose

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to something easy to read past. **Musa reverses the sequence.** Pharaoh raised the upbringing first and the killing second; Musa answers the killing first (ayat 20–21) and the upbringing last (ayah 22).

Why? Because in the Egyptian's case **there was a weakness on his part** — and he took that first. Present-day tactics, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes, avoid the direct reply and confuse the issue, mixing a weakness in so that it is camouflaged. Musa does the opposite. Being a messenger of Allah he had nothing to hide, so he **accepted his weakness and did not care in the least what the opposition would think of that admission** — even if they read it as a concession of defeat.

And consider the alternative that was available. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses this hard: Musa could have taken the simple, straightforward course and claimed the Egyptian deserved death, levelling accusations that would make the killing the right action. **There was no one present at the incident. No one could have contradicted him.** Anyone else in his place would certainly have taken that road. But here was the resolute messenger of Allah, "the truth personified", who regarded the plain declaration of fact as itself his victory. **He accepted his guilt in the packed court of his foe** — and in doing so, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, he countered any possibility of doubt about his prophethood. A man who will testify against himself before a hostile king is not a man who fabricates.

## "I did it then, when I was in error" (ayah 20)

Two words carry this ayah. *Idhan* — Ibn Kathir: it means **at that time**, marking off a closed chapter.

And *min al-ḍāllīn*, rendered "in error" or "lacking guidance". Ibn Kathir gives the boundary precisely: **"before revelation was sent to me and before Allah made me a Prophet and sent me with this Message."** Musa is locating the act in the period before prophethood, before the guidance of revelation had reached him.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the crucial qualification: while Musa accepted the fault — it was his misjudgment that he struck the Egyptian, and as a result the man died — **he made it very clear that he did not intend to kill him.** His intention was right; the purpose of the blow was to prevent the Egyptian from harming the Israelite, and the death was the outcome, not the aim. Hence, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes, this act of his, despite being wrong, **does not conflict with his claim to be a prophet or contradict its veracity.**

Notice what an honest admission actually looks like: he concedes the deed, refuses to invent an excuse for it, and at the same time refuses to accept a description of it that is false. Owning a mistake is not the same as accepting your accuser's version of it.

## "So I fled from you when I feared you" (ayah 21)

He does not dress the flight up as strategy. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān summarises his words: he realised his mistake and left the city for fear of being caught — and then Allah was kind to him and honoured him with prophethood.

Then the turn: *fa-wahaba lī rabbī ḥukman wa jaʿalanī min al-mursalīn* — "but my Lord has granted me *Hukm*, and made me one of the Messengers." Note whom he credits: *rabbī*, "my Lord". Pharaoh has just claimed the whole of Musa's making for himself; Musa answers by naming the One who actually gave him what matters.

Ibn Kathir reads the ayah as a statement of two eras: **"the first situation came to an end and another took its place."** And then the implication he draws out for Pharaoh, unsoftened: *Now Allah has sent me to you, and if you obey Him, you will be safe, but if you oppose Him, you will be destroyed.* The fugitive who once ran from this court is standing in it delivering terms.

## The favour handed back (ayah 22)

Now Musa turns to Pharaoh's first point — the upbringing Pharaoh had pressed in order to remind him of his favour. And the sentence is loaded: *And this is the past favour with which you reproach me — that you have enslaved the Children of Israel.*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces the logic Musa invites Pharaoh to follow. As an Israelite, Musa **had no occasion to reach the royal palace of Pharaoh at all.** He arrived there because Pharaoh's own cruelty compelled his mother to throw her baby into the river; Pharaoh then picked him up by chance; and in reality it was a wise arrangement made by Allah, so that **the very child for fear of whom Pharaoh had slaughtered thousands of children was caused to be nourished by Pharaoh himself.** The real cause of Musa's upbringing in that house, in any case, was the cruelty Pharaoh exercised against the Israelites. Pointing to this, Musa invites him to ponder whether this was really a favour he was obliging him with.

Ibn Kathir puts the arithmetic starkly: **whatever favours you did in bringing me up are offset by the evil you did by enslaving the Children of Israel and using them to do your hard labor. Is there any comparison between your favors to one man among them and the evil you have done to all of them? What you have mentioned about me is nothing compared to what you have done to them.** One childhood against six hundred and thirty thousand people in four hundred years of bondage. The ledger does not balance; it collapses.

## What it did to the room

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes with the effect of this address on the court. It left a positive and convincing impression on the minds of those present: they were convinced that Musa **was not the sort of person who would make excuses, and that he would say nothing but the truth** — a conviction confirmed further when they later saw the miracles. Pharaoh himself did not admit the truth, yet he was so overwhelmed and apprehensive that he feared these two men, without the support of even a third, would turn him and his people out of their land and country.

This, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, is **the Allah-given awe of truth, veracity and reality.** The contentions and dialectics of Allah's messengers are full of truth and of genuine well-wishing for the very person they address — and that is how they become so appealing to people, and how they convince the biggest defiant.

## Living it

- **Answer the argument, not the person.** Pharaoh's method — when you cannot meet the claim, go after the claimant's past — is instantly recognisable. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān flags it as the move of an opponent who lacks the arguments; refusing to use it is part of what makes debate a tool for reform instead of a contest.
- **Take your weakest point first, and tell the truth about it.** Musa had a real fault in his history and a perfect opportunity to lie about it, with no witness who could contradict him. He confessed it in his enemy's court — and that honesty removed any doubt about his prophethood.
- **Do not let a favour become a leash.** Pharaoh listed his kindnesses in order to ask, "so how can you have the face to speak before us?" Ayah 22 refuses the bargain: a good turn used to silence someone about a mass injustice does not survive being weighed against it.
- **Do not let your past disqualify your present.** "My Lord has granted me *Hukm*" — as Ibn Kathir puts it, the first situation came to an end and another took its place.

passages.title: "And what is the Lord of all worlds?"
passages.tafsir:
This passage is a debate, recorded almost like a transcript. Musa, peace be upon him, has just told Fir'awn that he is the messenger of "the Lord of all worlds" — and in ayah 23 Fir'awn throws the phrase back at him as a question. What holds ayat 23–28 together is the rhythm of that exchange: three times Musa, peace be upon him, answers by pointing at creation, and twice Fir'awn interrupts without ever touching the argument — first turning to his courtiers, then calling Musa a madman. It is a portrait of what truth sounds like under pressure, and of what a man does when he has power but no answer.

## What Fir'awn was really asking (ayah 23)

The question in ayah 23 — *wa mā rabbu-l-ʿālamīn*, "And what is the Lord of all worlds?" — sounds like a request for information. Ibn Kathir reads it as something else entirely. Fir'awn was the man who told his people, "I know not that you have a god other than me" (28:38), and of whom Allah says, "Thus he fooled his people, and they obeyed him" (43:54). His people used to deny the Creator, and they believed they had no other lord than Fir'awn. So when Musa, peace be upon him, said, "I am the Messenger of the Lord of the worlds," Fir'awn's question meant, in Ibn Kathir's paraphrase: *Who is this who you are claiming is the Lord of all worlds, other than me?* It is a challenge dressed as a query. Ibn Kathir notes that this is how the scholars of the Salaf and the Imams of later generations interpreted it, and As-Suddi points to the parallel scene in Sūrah Ṭā Hā, where Fir'awn asks, "Who then, O Musa, is the Lord of you two?" and Musa, peace be upon him, answers, "Our Lord is He Who gave to each thing its form and nature, then guided it aright" (20:49–50).

**A correction worth noticing.** Ibn Kathir pauses to reject a reading advanced by some among the philosophers and others: that this was a question about the *nature or substance* of Allah. They are mistaken, he says, because Fir'awn did not believe in the Creator in the first place, so he was in no position to ask about the nature of the Creator; he denied that the Creator existed at all, even though proof and evidence had been established against him. This matters for how we read the whole exchange. Musa, peace be upon him, is not being drawn into speculation about Allah's essence. He is being asked to justify the existence of a Lord above the throne of Egypt — and everything he says next is aimed at exactly that.

## Musa's first answer: the whole of creation (ayah 24)

Notice that Musa, peace be upon him, does not answer "what" with a definition. He answers by pointing at everything there is: "The Lord of the heavens and the earth, and all that is between them."

Ibn Kathir unfolds it in three registers, and it is worth slowing down to feel the sweep. There is the higher realm — the heavenly bodies within it, both those that are stationary and those that move and shine brightly. There is the lower realm — the oceans and continents, the mountains, trees, animals, plants and fruits. And there is what lies between the two — the winds, the birds, whatever is in the air. The point, in Ibn Kathir's words, is that this is the Creator, the Sovereign and Controller of all of it, their Deity Who has no partner or associate, the One Who has created all things. And all of them, from the stars to the birds, are servants to Him, submitting and humbling themselves before Him.

Put yourself in that throne room. Fir'awn's claim to lordship rested on an audience — a court, a people, a river valley. The answer of Musa, peace be upon him, quietly widens the frame until Egypt is a detail. Nothing in the sentence attacks Fir'awn; the sentence simply makes him small by being true.

**"If you seek to be convinced with certainty."** That is the clause that closes ayah 24, and Ibn Kathir glosses it: *if you have believing hearts and clear insight*. It is a condition, not a taunt. The evidence is the same for everyone; what differs is the heart brought to it. Musa, peace be upon him, is telling the court that the argument he has just made will only land on someone who actually wants to be convinced.

## The first interruption: playing to the room (ayah 25)

Fir'awn does not answer. He turns — and the ayah is careful to say to *whom* he turns: those around him, whom Ibn Kathir identifies as the chiefs and leaders of his state. "Do you not hear?" Ibn Kathir says he said this mockingly, expressing his disbelief in Musa, peace be upon him, and paraphrases the sneer: *are you not amazed by what this man is claiming — that you have another god other than me?*

This is one of the most recognisable moves in the passage. Evidence has been offered; Fir'awn responds by inviting the room to laugh. He shifts the question from *is it true* to *isn't he ridiculous*, because the second question he can win and the first he cannot.

## Musa's second answer: your Lord, and your fathers' (ayah 26)

The reply of Musa, peace be upon him, is aimed at the very people Fir'awn has just addressed, and it is one short phrase: "Your Lord and the Lord of your ancient fathers!" Ibn Kathir explains the meaning: the One Who created you and your forefathers, those who came before Fir'awn and his time.

Feel the pressure in that last clause. The court is being reminded that generations lived and died before this throne existed, and that whoever brought those generations into being was already their Lord. Fir'awn's own ancestors are on the list. His lordship, whatever else it is, arrived late in the story. And notice that the argument has moved from the cosmic to the personal: not merely Lord of the heavens, but *your* Lord, the One you already came from.

## The second interruption: attack the man (ayah 27)

Having failed to answer the heavens and failed to answer the ancestors, Fir'awn says: "Verily, your Messenger who has been sent to you is a madman!" Ibn Kathir gives the meaning: *there is no sense in his claim that there is any god other than me.*

Note again who he is speaking to. He does not say "you are mad"; he says "*your* Messenger... sent to *you*" — still addressing the court, still speaking about Musa, peace be upon him, rather than to him. And notice what the accusation actually contains: no counter-evidence, only the assertion that anyone who says there is a god besides Fir'awn is talking nonsense. Where one claim has been made the only sane position, disagreement itself becomes proof of madness.

## Musa's third answer: then reverse the sunrise (ayah 28)

Musa, peace be upon him, does not defend himself. He takes the same argument up one more level: "Lord of the east and the west, and all that is between them, if you did but understand!"

Ibn Kathir draws out why this particular pair of directions. He is the One Who made the east the place where the heavenly bodies rise and made the west the place where they set; this is the system to which He has subjugated all the heavenly bodies, the stationary and the moving alike. And then the unspoken challenge, which Ibn Kathir voices: if what Fir'awn claims is true, that he is your lord and your god, *then let him turn things around, so that the heavenly bodies set in the east and rise in the west.*

It is evidence that every person in that hall could check for themselves, and that no one could imitate. Ibn Kathir points to the twin of this moment in Sūrah al-Baqarah: the man who disputed with Ibrahim about his Lord because Allah had given him the kingdom. Ibrahim said, "My Lord is He Who gives life and causes death." He said, "I give life and cause death." So Ibrahim said, "Verily, Allah brings the sun from the east. So cause it to rise from the west" (2:258). In both scenes a ruler is invited to demonstrate the lordship he claims, and in both the claim dies in the silence that follows.

**Who is being addressed.** Ayah 24 closed on a condition — "if you seek to be convinced with certainty," which Ibn Kathir explains as believing hearts and clear insight. Ayah 28 closes on another: "if you did but understand!" And Ibn Kathir tells us who these last words were spoken to — those in whose hearts Fir'awn had planted doubts. There were listeners in that room, and they are still being addressed.

And that is where the passage lands. Ibn Kathir's summary of what follows is stark: when Fir'awn was defeated in debate, he resorted to the use of his force and power, believing that this would be effective in dealing with Musa, peace be upon him. The threat that comes in the next ayah is not a new argument. It is the admission that he has none.

## Behind the debate

The exchange did not happen in a vacuum. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Qurtubi, fills in the background to the demand Musa, peace be upon him, had already made in ayah 17 — "that you must send the children of Isra'il with us." Bani Isra'il were residents of Syria. They wanted to go back to their land, but Fir'awn would not let them. Four hundred years had passed with them living in his bondage like slaves, and by then they numbered six hundred and thirty thousand. When Musa, peace be upon him, presented the message of truth to Fir'awn, he also asked him to stop all the cruelties he had perpetrated against Bani Isra'il and to let them go home. So the confrontation in which ayah 23 is spoken is not a seminar. Real lives were waiting on its outcome.

## How a prophet argues

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a longer lesson from this scene under the heading of *munāẓarah* — the conventional term for formal debate or dialectic. Its observation is that such debate has been reduced to a game of win or lose: a man keeps pressing his point though he knows he is in the wrong, uses his intelligence to throw in all sorts of arguments to prove himself correct, and rejects his opponent's point with full force even when that point is right. Islam, it says, sets out rules for this and turns it back into a useful tool for preaching and reform.

Its example is how this very confrontation opened. When a sharp opponent is not properly equipped with correct arguments, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, he normally tries to switch the conversation towards the person of the addressee in order to find fault with him — a tactic used to embarrass him and make him look small before the audience. That is precisely how Fir'awn began, before ayah 23, with two personal points rather than arguments. The reply of Musa, peace be upon him, was the opposite instinct: he had nothing to hide, and he regarded the declaration of fact as his victory. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes the effect on the room — the people present were convinced that he was not the sort of person who would make excuses, and that he would say nothing but the truth. This, it concludes, is the awe that Allah places in truth and reality: the contentions and dialectics of Allah's messengers are full of truth and of genuine well-wishing for the person addressed, which is how they become so appealing to people and convince the biggest defiant.

## Living it

**Answer the question, not the audience.** The three replies (ayat 24, 26, 28) are one answer made more concrete each time: the heavens, then your own fathers, then the east and the west. When someone will not engage, do not raise your voice — bring the evidence to something they cannot pretend to miss.

**Expect the ridicule, and do not let it change the subject.** Both of Fir'awn's lines (ayat 25 and 27) try to move the conversation from *is this true* to *is this man foolish*. Being mocked is not the same as being refuted. In this whole passage, Musa, peace be upon him, never once defends his own dignity; he keeps returning to Allah.

**Let the truth be your victory.** The striking thing Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies is a messenger who regarded the plain declaration of fact as his victory, and who was believed afterwards because of it. Honesty offered without spin is not a loss of the argument. It is what makes everything else you say believable.

**Remember who you are really speaking to.** Ibn Kathir says the last answer was addressed to those in whose hearts Fir'awn had planted doubts. Some people will not be convinced. The listeners around them still might be — and they are reason enough to keep speaking with evidence, patience, and goodwill.

passages.title: The threat of prison and the two signs
passages.tafsir:
**The passage in one breath.** A tyrant who has lost an argument reaches for the one thing he still controls — the prison door. Musa (peace be upon him) does not flinch or shout back; he answers with a question. And Allah answers Pharaoh's threat with two signs that no throne can argue with: a staff that becomes a serpent, and a hand that comes out shining.

What holds ayat 29–33 together is a single unbroken exchange in Pharaoh's own court, moving in four quick steps: the threat (29), Musa's calm counter-question (30), Pharaoh's dare (31), and the two signs delivered on the spot (32–33). Ibn Kathir gives the movement its title: **after the rational proof, Pharaoh resorts to force.**

## Where we are in the story

Musa and Harun (peace be upon them) have come into the court of a king who claimed to be a god, carrying a demand as well as a message. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Qurtubi, fills in what that demand meant on the ground: Bani Israʼil were residents of Syria who wanted to return to their own land, and Pharaoh would not let them. Four hundred years had passed with them living in his bondage like slaves, and by that time they numbered six hundred and thirty thousand. So when Musa presented the message of truth, he also asked Pharaoh to stop the cruelties he had perpetrated against Bani Israʼil and to let them go to their homeland.

That is the request sitting on the table when ayah 29 is spoken. It is not an abstract theological debate. It is a demand that the empire release the people it had enslaved.

Before this, Pharaoh had tried to fight on the level of argument — and, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out, he had done it in the way weak debaters do: when a sharp opponent is not properly equipped with correct arguments, he switches the conversation to the *person* of the one he is addressing, hunting for faults, to embarrass him and make him look small before the audience. Pharaoh raised two such personal points: *we brought you up in our household and did you so many favours*, and *you killed an Egyptian* — cruelty and ingratitude in one charge.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān dwells on how Musa answered, because it is a model of what debate is supposed to be. He changed the sequence, taking up the killing first even though Pharaoh had raised it second — the point where he was weakest. He did not camouflage it. He accepted that it was his misjudgement, while making very clear that he had not intended to kill: he had struck the man to prevent him harming an Israelite, and the death followed, which was not the intention. And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes what he *could* have done instead: there was no one present at the incident, so no one could have contradicted him had he simply claimed the Egyptian deserved death. Anyone else in his place would certainly have taken that course. But here was the resolute messenger of Allah, who regarded the declaration of fact as his victory — and by accepting his guilt in the packed court of his foe, he countered any possibility of doubt being raised against his prophethood.

Then he turned to the favour of his upbringing, and invited Pharaoh to ponder how an Israelite ever came to reach the royal palace at all: it was Pharaoh's own cruelty that compelled his mother to put her baby into the river, and in reality a wise arrangement by Allah, so that the very child for fear of whom Pharaoh had slaughtered thousands of children was nourished by Pharaoh himself. So — was this really a favour you are obliging me with?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the conclusion: this prophetic address left a positive and convincing impression on the minds of the people present. They were convinced that Musa was not the sort of person who would make excuses, and that he would say nothing but the truth.

## Ayah 29 — the threat

**"If you take a god other than me, I will certainly put you among the prisoners."**

Ibn Kathir's reading is exact: proof had been established against Pharaoh, clearly and rationally, so he resorted to using force against Musa — thinking that after this there would be no further room for discussion. That last phrase is worth pausing on. The threat is not an argument; it is a way of *ending* arguments. A man who is winning does not need a dungeon.

Notice too what he demands. Not that Musa stop preaching, not that he drop the request about Bani Israʼil, but that he not "take a god other than me." Pharaoh has heard the message clearly. He knows the dispute is over lordship, and he states it as a straight choice between two claimants to it.

## Ayah 30 — "Even if I bring you something manifest?"

**Awalaw jiʼtuka bi-shayʼin mubīn** — "Even if I bring you something manifest?"

Ibn Kathir glosses **mubīn** here as *clear and definitive proof*.

Read the tone of the reply. There is no defiance, no counter-threat, no appeal for mercy. Musa answers a threat of prison with a question about evidence — which is to say, he refuses to leave the ground of proof even after his opponent has abandoned it. The threat simply does not move him off his subject.

## Ayah 31 — the dare

**"Bring it forth then, if you are of the truthful!"**

Pharaoh answers with a challenge, and the word he reaches for is **al-ṣādiqīn**, the truthful. He makes truthfulness the test — which is precisely the ground on which, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān showed, Musa had already made his impression on that court: the man who accepted his own fault in an enemy's hall is now asked to prove he is not a liar. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that after the people saw the miracles, their view of him was confirmed further.

## Ayat 32–33 — the two signs

**"So he threw his stick, and behold, it was a serpent, manifest. And he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white to all beholders."**

The Qur'an gives the two signs in two short clauses with no build-up. No spell, no ritual, no delay. He throws; it is a serpent. He draws out his hand; it is shining.

**The serpent.** Ibn Kathir describes it as very clear and obvious — with a huge body and a big mouth, terrifying in appearance. The word **mubīn** returns here, and it is worth noticing: Musa had offered "something *mubīn*" in ayah 30, and what lands on the floor of the throne room in ayah 32 is a serpent *mubīn*. The promise and the proof are described with the same word. Nobody in that hall could say they had not seen it or could not make out what it was.

**The hand.** Ibn Kathir explains **wa-nazaʿa yadahu**, "and he drew out his hand," as meaning *from his sleeve*, and describes what appeared: it was shining like a piece of the moon. The Qur'an adds **lil-nāẓirīn**, "to all beholders" — the sign is described in terms of the eyes watching it. This was not something Musa experienced privately and then reported; it was seen.

Notice how different the two are from one another: one terrifying in appearance, one shining like a piece of the moon.

## What Pharaoh did with the proof

Ibn Kathir's comment on the response is severe and clarifying. **Since Pharaoh was already doomed, he hastened to stubborn denial** — telling the chiefs around him that this was a well-versed sorcerer, one who knows a great deal of magic, trying to convince them that what they had just watched was sorcery and not a miracle. This is the oldest move against clear evidence: not to refute it, but to rename it.

And yet look at what had happened to the man who, moments before, was promising to put Musa among the prisoners. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names it: Pharaoh did not admit the truth, yet he was so overwhelmed and apprehensive that he feared two men, without the support of a third, would turn him and his people out of their land and country. This is what Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls the Allah-given awe of truth, veracity and reality — the contentions of Allah's messengers are full of truth and of wishing well for the very person addressed, and that is how they become so appealing to people and convince the biggest defiant.

## Living it

**Notice when the argument ends and the threat begins.** Ayah 29 marks the exact moment: force arrives when proof runs out. When someone answers evidence with intimidation, mockery, or a change of subject onto your person and your past, the Qur'an is showing you that this is the signature of a losing position.

**Answer the threat by staying on the subject.** Musa's reply in ayah 30 is one short question about evidence. He does not defend himself, insult back, or plead. If you have the truth, keep pointing at it.

**Debate to reach the truth, not to win.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān contrasts two attitudes. In the common approach, *munāzarah* — formal debate — has been reduced to a game of win or lose: keep pressing your point even knowing you are on the wrong, throw in every argument you can find, and reject your opponent's point with full force even when it is correct. Islam has given a middle-of-the-road stance, with rules that make debate a useful tool for preaching and reform. Musa gives us the pattern: take up the hardest charge against you first, accept what you actually got wrong, clarify only what is genuinely false, and let the truth do the persuading. His honesty did not weaken his case — it convinced the room that he would say nothing but the truth, and the miracles then confirmed their view further.

**And do not measure the outcome by the opponent's reaction.** Pharaoh saw a serpent on his own floor and a hand shining like a piece of the moon, and called it magic. Clear proof does not convert a heart that has hastened to stubborn denial. But the proof was still worth giving: the court saw it, and the record of it is being recited to us thousands of years later.

passages.title: Pharaoh brands Moses a skilled magician
passages.tafsir:
A tyrant has just watched two undeniable signs, and instead of yielding he reaches for a word. In these four ayat Pharaoh turns to the noblemen seated around him, brands Mūsā (peace be upon him) a skilled magician, and re-frames a matter of truth as a matter of national security — and his courtiers answer with a plan that will, without their knowing it, stage the very confrontation Allah intended.

What holds ayat 34–37 together is that they are all *reaction*: not a rebuttal of the proof, but a management of the room.

## The scene into which ayah 34 speaks

Ibn Kathir places these ayat immediately after the proof has landed. His heading for the passage is blunt: **after the rational proof, Fir'awn resorts to force.** Once the argument had been established against Pharaoh "clearly and rationally," he threatened prison — and when Mūsā answered by producing what Ibn Kathir calls "clear and definitive proof," the staff and the shining hand, the court fell silent.

Then Pharaoh opens his mouth.

## Ayah 34 — the word chosen instead of the truth

**"He said to the chiefs around him: 'Verily, this is indeed a well-versed sorcerer.'"**

Ibn Kathir's reading of Pharaoh's inner state is unsparing: "Since Fir'awn was already doomed, he hastened to stubborn denial." The phrase *sāḥir ʿalīm* means, Ibn Kathir explains, "one who knows a great deal of magic or witchcraft." Notice what the label concedes. Pharaoh does not say *nothing happened*; he does not deny what the court has just seen. He grants the phenomenon and re-files it under a heading his court already has a folder for. Ibn Kathir states the purpose plainly: "Fir'awn was trying to convince them that this was sorcery, not a miracle."

Two details of the wording repay attention.

First, **to whom** he speaks. The ayah says he spoke "to the chiefs around him." He does not answer Mūsā. He turns away from the man who produced the proof and addresses the audience. An argument he cannot win is converted into an audience he can still hold.

Second, the emphasis. Ibn Kathir's rendering carries it: "Verily, this is *indeed* a well-versed sorcerer" — a heavily stressed assertion. The heavier the assertion, the less evidence stands behind it. A man with proof states it once; a man without proof insists.

And there is a bitter irony in the gloss Ibn Kathir gives — "one who knows a great deal." Pharaoh cannot bring himself to call Mūsā a fraud or a fool. Even his slander is a backhanded testimony to the sheer quality of what he has just seen.

## Ayah 35 — from "he is lying" to "he is dangerous"

**"He wants to drive you out of your land by his sorcery: what is it then that you command?"**

This is the sentence that changes the subject. Ibn Kathir says that having labelled Mūsā, Pharaoh "provoked them against Musa, trying to make them oppose him and disbelieve in him," and he unpacks the accusation in Pharaoh's own logic: *he wants to capture the people's hearts and win them over by doing this, so that they will support him, and help him and follow him, and he will defeat you in your own land and take the land from you.*

Look carefully at the pronoun. Pharaoh does not say *my* land — he says **your** land. He is not asking the nobles to defend his throne; he is telling them their own standing, their own country, is at stake. Ibn Kathir's paraphrase makes the pitch explicit: *he will defeat you in your own land and take the land from you.* The dispute over who deserves worship is quietly turned into a dispute over property. That is how a threatened power recruits: it convinces the comfortable that the truth-teller is coming for *their* house.

And notice what has vanished. The threat that opened this exchange was about divinity — "if you choose a god other than me." Ayah 35 says nothing about gods at all. The theological claim has been dropped without being defended, because it could not be defended, and a political one has taken its place.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a striking psychological note about this very moment. The earlier exchange — Pharaoh's two personal jabs about Mūsā's upbringing in the palace and about the Egyptian he had struck, and Mūsā's honest, unevasive reply — had left the court convinced that this was a man who "would say nothing but the truth," and the signs then confirmed that impression. So Maʿārif observes: "although the Pharaoh did not admit the truth, yet he was so overwhelmed and apprehensive that just two persons without having the support of a third, would turn him and his people out of their land and country." The fear in ayah 35 is real. Pharaoh is not merely inventing a scare for the nobles; he genuinely felt it. Maʿārif names what is happening: this is what is known as the Allah-given awe of truth, veracity and reality — the weight that reality carries even in the chest of a man determined to reject it.

There is also a concrete stake behind "your land." Maʿārif, citing Qurṭubī, notes that the demand Mūsā had brought was that the Children of Israel be sent with him (26:17). They were originally residents of Syria who wanted to return to their land, but Pharaoh would not let them; four hundred years had passed with them living in his bondage like slaves, and by then they numbered six hundred and thirty thousand. Mūsā had asked Pharaoh to stop the cruelties he had perpetrated over them and to let them go to their homeland. That is the request Pharaoh reports to his court as an attempt to drive the Egyptians out of their own land.

**"What is it then that you command?"** Pause on this. The man who had just said "a god other than me" is now putting the decision in his courtiers' hands; Ibn Kathir paraphrases the sense as, "So advise me, what should I do with him?" The claimed deity is out of ideas and asking for instructions. Nothing in these four ayat exposes the hollowness of his claim more efficiently than his own question.

## Ayat 36–37 — the courtiers' plan

**"They said: 'Put him off and his brother, and send callers to the cities, to bring up to you every well-versed sorcerer.'"**

Ibn Kathir gives the sense of the advice: "delay him and his brother until you gather together all the sorcerers from every city and region of your kingdom so that they may confront him and produce something like he produces, then you will defeat him and have the victory."

Three things are worth seeing here.

**The threat of prison quietly dies.** The exchange had opened with Pharaoh promising jail. Now the advice is: don't imprison him, delay him. The nobles understand that a claim can only be beaten in public by a rival claim.

**"His brother" is counted in without being named.** Hārūn (peace be upon him) has not spoken in this passage, yet the court includes him in its calculations. Maʿārif notes that Mūsā and Hārūn together conveyed the invitation of Truth into Pharaoh's court. Two men — and an empire has to convene a national programme against them.

**The scale of the mobilisation.** The men to be sent out are described in the ayah's own rendering as callers, mobilisers — Ibn Kathir has "send callers to the cities" — and the plan is to sweep "every city and region of your kingdom" for *every* well-versed sorcerer. You do not empty a kingdom of its best specialists to debunk a conjurer. The size of the response tells you how seriously they took what they had seen.

## The plan that served Allah's purpose

Then comes the line in Ibn Kathir that turns the whole passage around:

"So Fir'awn did as they suggested, which is what Allah decreed would happen to them, so that all the people would gather in one place and the signs and proof of Allah would be made manifest before them all in one day."

The court believed it was designing Mūsā's humiliation. What it was actually doing was building the stage, printing the invitations and guaranteeing the attendance for the public vindication of Allah's messenger. Every rider dispatched to every city was, unknowingly, working for the side he was sent to destroy. Pharaoh asks his nobles what to command; their command executes a decree that was never theirs.

This is a quiet, enormous comfort for anyone who feels outmatched by the machinery arrayed against the truth. The machinery runs on Allah's decree. The plot is not merely defeated afterwards — it is *used*.

## Living it

**The oldest trick against a messenger is a label.** Pharaoh never engaged the evidence; he gave it a name — "sorcery" — and moved on. It is the cheapest move available to a person who is losing, and it still works: call an argument a conspiracy theory, a fanaticism, a phase, and you never have to answer it. Ibn Kathir's diagnosis is the antidote — Pharaoh was "trying to convince them that this was sorcery, not a miracle." When you notice yourself reaching for a category instead of a reply, examine what you are avoiding.

**Watch for the switch from truth to threat.** The moment a claim cannot be answered on its merits, it gets recast as a danger to the audience's interests: your land, your standing, your way of life. Ayah 35 is the template. Recognising it in others is useful; recognising it in yourself is necessary.

**Argue like a prophet, not like a debater.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws exactly this lesson from the wider exchange. Debate — *munāẓarah* in the classical vocabulary, meaning formal dialectic between people who hold opposing views — has been reduced, Maʿārif says, to "a game of win or lose": people keep pressing a point they know to be wrong, throw in all sorts of arguments to prove it correct, and reject the opponent's point with full force even when it is right. Islam, in contrast, sets out rules that make debate "a useful tool for preaching and reform."

The model is Mūsā's own conduct. Pharaoh had opened with two personal attacks — the favour of being raised in his household, and the Egyptian who had died at Mūsā's hand — because, as Maʿārif notes, an opponent not properly equipped with correct arguments switches the conversation toward the person of the addressee to find faults with him: "This tactic is employed to embarrass the opponent and to make him look small before the audience." Mūsā answered the harder charge first — the one Pharaoh had raised second, and the one where he was weakest — rather than burying it. He accepted that it was a misjudgement, while making clear he had not intended to kill: the purpose of striking the man was to prevent him from harming the Israelite, and the death was not the intention.

Maʿārif points out how easily he could have done otherwise. He could have claimed the Egyptian deserved death and levelled charges to justify it; no one had been present at the incident, so no one could have contradicted him. "Anyone else in his place would have certainly taken this course of action." Instead, being the resolute messenger of Allah, "he regarded expression of truth and veracity and the declaration of fact as his victory." By accepting his fault in the packed court of his foe, he "countered any possibility of doubt on his prophethood" — the admission removed suspicion rather than raising it.

That is the standard: your victory is that the truth was said, not that you were seen to win. Maʿārif's closing observation is that the contentions of Allah's messengers "are also full of truth, veracity and wishing well for the addressee" — even Pharaoh was being wished well, not merely defeated — "and that is how they become so appealing to people and convince the biggest defiant."

**And the awe of truth is real even in those who reject it.** Pharaoh denied with his tongue what had already unsettled his heart. Do not measure the effect of the truth you speak by whether the other person concedes. Sometimes the loudest denial is the sound of something landing.

passages.title: The magicians assemble and bargain for reward
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat are the *staging* of the great contest between Musa (peace be upon him) and the magicians of Egypt: a day is fixed, a nation is summoned to watch, the magicians arrive at the royal court and — before a single rope is thrown — stop to negotiate their fee. Nothing miraculous happens yet. What holds the passage together is that it shows us, step by step, how falsehood organises itself when it feels threatened: it sets the terms, gathers a crowd, and buys its champions.

## The setting Ibn Kathir puts before us

Ibn Kathir frames this whole episode in one sentence before he comments on a single word: "The Egyptians wanted to extinguish the Light of Allah with their words, but Allah insisted that His Light should prevail even though the disbelievers disliked that." He then adds a principle worth memorising: this is the issue of disbelief and faith — *they never confront one another but faith always prevails*. He supports it with two ayat from elsewhere in the Qur'an:

> "Nay, We fling the truth against the falsehood, so it destroys it, and behold, it disappears. And woe to you for that which you ascribe." (21:18)

> "And say: 'Truth has come and falsehood has vanished.'" (17:81)

Hold that in mind as you read ayat 38–42, because on the surface these ayat read like a story going badly for the believers. The state has the timetable, the venue, the crowd, the payroll, and the finest practitioners in the land. Ibn Kathir notes that the sorcerers of Egypt were the most skilled in the art of illusion, and that a huge group of them gathered from all corners of the land. The reader is being shown falsehood at the very height of its organisation — precisely so that its collapse a few ayat later is unmistakable.

## Ayah 38 — assembled at a set time on an appointed day

*Fa-jumiʿa al-saḥaratu li-mīqāti yawmin maʿlūm.*

"So, the sorcerers were assembled at a fixed time on a day appointed."

The ayah does not say the magicians came; it says they *were assembled*. They are moved into position by someone else — Ibn Kathir notes, a few lines later, that it was Fir'awn who "had brought them together" for this matter. That is the first quiet irony of the passage: the men who are about to be publicly celebrated as champions of the realm begin as people summoned by a king.

And the day is fixed and known. This was not a private test in a palace back room; it was an announced, national occasion.

Ibn Kathir's comment on that day is striking in its restraint. Speaking of the enormous crowd that assembled, he describes it as that day "whose exact numbers are known to Allah Alone." The classical commentator will not guess at figures the revelation did not give. That reticence is itself a lesson in how to handle the details of sacred history: where Allah has been silent, the scholar stays silent.

## Ayat 39–40 — the crowd that would follow whoever won

*Wa qīla li-l-nāsi hal antum mujtamiʿūn — laʿallanā nattabiʿu al-saḥarata in kānū humu al-ghālibīn.*

"And it was said to the people: 'Are you (too) going to assemble?' — 'That we may follow the sorcerers if they are the winners.'"

Ibn Kathir puts his finger exactly on the disease in the people's answer. Introducing their words — "That we may follow the sorcerers if they are the winners" — he observes:

> "They did not say: 'we will follow the truth, whether it rests with the sorcerers or with Musa;' the people were followers of the religion of their king."

Read that slowly, because it is the sharpest sentence in the whole passage. Their loyalty was committed before the evidence was seen. The one thing they never considered saying was, *we will follow whoever turns out to be right*. Their formula binds them to a side and then hopes that side wins. Ibn Kathir names the cause without softening it: their religion was the religion of whoever sat on the throne. Power decided truth for them; truth was never allowed to decide anything.

Notice, too, the word the crowd reaches for: **al-ghālibīn** — "the winners," "those who overcome." It is the same word the magicians will use in the very next ayah when they set their price. Everyone in this scene is thinking in terms of *winning*. Not one of them, in these ayat, is recorded as thinking in terms of *being right*.

## Ayah 41 — the bargain

*Fa-lammā jāʾa al-saḥaratu qālū li-Firʿawna a-inna lanā la-ajran in kunnā naḥnu al-ghālibīn.*

"So, when the sorcerers arrived, they said to Fir'awn: 'Will there surely be a reward for us if we are the winners?'"

Ibn Kathir fills in the scene. "When the sorcerers arrived" means when they reached the court of Fir'awn, where a pavilion had been erected for him; there he had gathered his servants, his followers, his administrators, his provincial leaders, and the soldiers of his kingdom. Picture it: a raised canopy, the ruler beneath it, the entire apparatus of the state arranged around him, and the nation gathered to watch.

And into that theatre the magicians walk and ask about their terms. Ibn Kathir describes what they were really after: they "stood before Fir'awn, asking him to treat them well and bring them closer to him if they prevailed in this matter which he had brought them together for."

These men have been called to stand against a Prophet of Allah, and their first recorded concern is the reward attached. They ask what is in it for them before they ask what is true.

There is a bitter symmetry worth noticing across these two ayat: the crowd in ayah 40 will follow whoever wins, and the magicians in ayah 41 will fight on the condition of a reward. Between them you have two great substitutes for conviction — siding with the strong, and serving the paymaster.

## Ayah 42 — "of those brought near"

*Qāla naʿam wa innakum idhan la-mina al-muqarrabīn.*

"He said: 'Yes, and you shall then verily be of those brought near (to myself).'"

Fir'awn does not merely agree; he raises the offer. Ibn Kathir explains his answer as meaning: "and you will be given more than what you are asking for; I will make you among those who are close to me, those who sit with me."

That is the currency of a court. Not simply payment, but nearness — being close to the ruler, seated with him. Fir'awn understands that what will secure these men is not only a reward but a place at his side. So the passage closes with the offer made and accepted, the crowd in position, the pavilion full, and the terms agreed.

Ibn Kathir's commentary carries straight on from here into what happened when all of this arrangement finally met Musa (peace be upon him) — but that is the business of the ayat that follow. Our five ayat end at the height of the staging, with everything apparently in Fir'awn's favour.

## Living it

**Settle in advance that you follow the truth, not the winner.** The people of ayah 40 were not evil geniuses; they were ordinary spectators who had already decided to side with whoever came out on top. Ibn Kathir's diagnosis — that they were "followers of the religion of their king" — describes a temptation that has not gone out of date. Ask yourself honestly whether your convictions would survive your side losing an argument in public.

**Watch what you are being offered.** Fir'awn's answer in ayah 42 was not crude. As Ibn Kathir renders it, it was an offer of more than they had asked for: *those who are close to me, those who sit with me*. Access, closeness, a place in the room. Where you find yourself softening a position you know to be true, it is worth asking what nearness you are protecting.

**Do not be intimidated by the scale of the staging.** Ayat 38–42 give falsehood every advantage — the king, the fixed day, the crowd, the most skilled practitioners in the land, the promised reward. Ibn Kathir's opening principle still holds over all of it: disbelief and faith never confront one another but faith always prevails. "Nay, We fling the truth against the falsehood, so it destroys it, and behold, it disappears."

passages.title: The magicians cast, believe, and defy Pharaoh
passages.tafsir:
These nine ayat are the contest itself and what came out of it: Musa invites the magicians to throw, they throw and swear by Fir'awn's might, Musa's staff swallows their illusion, and the very men hired to defeat him end the day face-down in prostration, telling the tyrant to do his worst. What holds the passage together is a single reversal — the men brought in as Fir'awn's weapon become, within the space of one confrontation, the first believers among his people, and their courage becomes a sign in its own right.

## A contest staged by a king

Ibn Kathir notes that Allah describes this encounter between Musa (peace be upon him) and the Egyptians in Surat al-A'raf, in Surah Ta Ha, and here — and that here the incident is described more briefly.

The setup, from the ayat just before ours: the magicians were assembled at a fixed time on an appointed day, the people were called to gather, and the crowd's stated hope was "that we may follow the sorcerers if they are the winners." Ibn Kathir puts his finger on that sentence. They did not say *we will follow the truth, whether it rests with the sorcerers or with Musa*. Their loyalty was to the winning side, because, as he says, the people were followers of the religion of their king.

When the magicians arrived, they reached the court of Fir'awn, where a pavilion had been erected for him and he had gathered his servants, followers, administrators, provincial leaders and the soldiers of his kingdom. The magicians stood before him asking to be treated well and brought closer to him if they prevailed. They asked, "Will there surely be a reward for us if we are the winners?" Fir'awn promised more than they asked — "you shall then verily be of those brought near," meaning, in Ibn Kathir's words, that they would be made among those close to him, those who sit with him.
